dram-vs-sram.title: DRAM vs SRAM: Key Differences Explained
dram-vs-sram.description: DRAM vs SRAM in one table: cell structure, refresh, speed, density, cost, power and typical uses, plus a guide to when each one is used.
dram-vs-sram.lead: DRAM stores each bit as charge on a tiny capacitor, so it is dense and cheap but must be refreshed. SRAM stores each bit in a latch built from transistors, so it is faster and needs no refresh, but takes much more area per bit. That is why computers use DRAM for large main memory and SRAM for small, fast caches.

CPU and GPU caches, register files and small on-chip buffers
when: DRAM
When you need a lot of memory at a low cost per bit and can tolerate some latency: main memory in PCs, servers and smartphones, and graphics memory for GPUs.
SRAM
When speed matters most and the capacity can be small: CPU caches, register files, and small buffers where you do not want refresh circuitry.
Together
Real computers use both. A fast SRAM cache holds frequently used data and hides the latency of the slower DRAM.
faq: Is SRAM faster than DRAM?

Yes. SRAM holds each bit in a latch of transistors, so on-chip SRAM can be accessed in about a nanosecond. DRAM must first activate a row and takes tens of nanoseconds, which is why SRAM is used for CPU caches.
Why is DRAM cheaper than SRAM?

A DRAM cell needs only one transistor and one capacitor, while an SRAM cell usually needs six transistors. The smaller cell packs far more bits into the same silicon area, which lowers the cost per bit.
Why does DRAM need refresh?

The capacitor in a DRAM cell slowly leaks its charge, so the data must be read and rewritten periodically, typically within 64 ms. SRAM keeps its value as long as power is applied, so it needs no refresh.
Is DRAM or SRAM non-volatile?
Neither. Both lose their data when power is removed. Non-volatile memories such as flash, MRAM and ReRAM keep their data without power.

nand-vs-nor-flash.title: NAND vs NOR Flash: Differences and Uses
nand-vs-nor-flash.description: NAND vs NOR flash memory compared in a table: cell connection, read and write speed, erase unit, density, cost, reliability and typical uses.
nand-vs-nor-flash.lead: Both are non-volatile flash memories, but they are wired differently. NOR flash connects its cells in parallel, so it offers fast random reads and can run code in place, but it is expensive per bit. NAND flash connects its cells in series, so it packs far more bits into the same area and is cheap, but it reads and writes in pages and needs error correction. That is why NAND stores your data and NOR stores firmware.

Cells are connected in parallel to the bit line, so each cell can be accessed directly

Programmed one page at a time; high throughput for sequential writes
Programmed in small units; slower for large amounts of data
Fowler-Nordheim tunneling for both program and erase
Channel hot-electron injection to program, tunneling to erase
High density and low cost; 3D NAND stacks hundreds of layers, and TLC/QLC store 3 to 4 bits per cell
Lower density (usually up to a few gigabits per chip) and higher cost per bit
No. Code must be copied to RAM first

From about 100,000 program/erase cycles (SLC) down to roughly 1,000 or fewer (QLC)
SSDs, USB drives, memory cards, smartphone storage (eMMC, UFS)
Boot code and firmware: BIOS/UEFI chips, microcontroller code, automotive and industrial devices
when: NAND flash
When you need a large amount of cheap, non-volatile storage and can read and write in pages: SSDs, phones, cameras, memory cards.
NOR flash
When you need to store program code that a processor reads directly and reliably, and the capacity is modest: boot ROM, firmware, small embedded systems.
Together
Many devices use both: a small NOR chip holds the boot code, which then loads the operating system from a large NAND device.
faq: Why is NAND flash cheaper than NOR flash?

NAND cells are connected in series strings and share contacts, so each bit takes much less area. Together with 3D stacking and multi-bit cells, this gives high density and a low cost per bit. NOR cells are wired in parallel and take more area.
Can a processor run code directly from NAND flash?
Not directly. NAND is read in pages and has bit errors, so code is usually copied to RAM first. NOR flash supports execute in place (XIP), which is why it stores boot code and firmware.
Which flash is used in SSDs and phones?
NAND flash. SSDs, USB drives, memory cards and phone storage such as eMMC and UFS all use NAND because of its low cost and high capacity.
Does NAND flash wear out faster than NOR?

Generally yes. NAND endurance ranges from about 100,000 cycles (SLC) down to around 1,000 (QLC), while NOR typically lasts around 100,000 cycles. NAND controllers use wear leveling and error correction to extend its life.

bjt-vs-mosfet.title: BJT vs MOSFET: Differences Explained
bjt-vs-mosfet.description: BJT vs MOSFET compared in a table: control method, input current, carriers, speed, on-state behavior, temperature behavior, integration and typical uses.
bjt-vs-mosfet.lead: A bipolar junction transistor (BJT) is controlled by a base current, while a MOSFET is controlled by the voltage on an insulated gate. That one difference explains most of the rest: MOSFETs draw almost no steady input current and are easy to integrate by the billions, which is why they dominate digital chips, while BJTs offer high transconductance and low noise, which keeps them useful in analog and RF circuits.

Voltage-controlled: gate voltage sets drain current

Analog amplifiers, RF circuits, bandgap references, simple discrete switches
Digital logic, memory, power switching, most modern ICs
when: BJT
When you need high gain per unit current, low noise or a precise voltage reference: analog front ends, audio and RF amplifiers, bandgap references.
MOSFET
When you need a switch or a very large number of devices on one chip: digital logic, memory, power converters, motor drives.
IGBT
The IGBT combines a MOS gate with a bipolar output stage. It is used where voltage and current are high, such as motor drives and inverters.
faq: What is the main difference between a BJT and a MOSFET?

A BJT is controlled by a base current, while a MOSFET is controlled by the voltage on an insulated gate. A MOSFET draws almost no steady gate current, which makes it easy to integrate in huge numbers.
Why are MOSFETs used in digital chips instead of BJTs?
MOSFETs are small and, in CMOS circuits, draw almost no static power. BJTs need bias current and take more area, so billions of them on one chip would overheat.
When is a BJT better than a MOSFET?
A BJT has higher transconductance for the same current and lower low-frequency noise, so it remains useful in analog amplifiers, RF circuits and bandgap voltage references.
What is an IGBT?
An IGBT combines a MOS gate with a bipolar output stage. It is used for high voltage and high current, such as motor drives and inverters, where it has lower conduction loss than a MOSFET.

finfet-vs-gaa.title: FinFET vs GAA Transistors: Key Differences
finfet-vs-gaa.description: FinFET vs gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors compared in a table: gate structure, channel, electrostatic control, width tuning, manufacturing and adoption.
finfet-vs-gaa.lead: In a FinFET the gate wraps a vertical fin of silicon on three sides. In a gate-all-around (GAA) transistor the gate surrounds the channel on all sides, usually as stacked horizontal nanosheets. Wrapping the channel more completely gives better control of leakage at short gate lengths, which is why leading chipmakers are moving from FinFET to GAA at the 3 nm and 2 nm class.

The gate surrounds the channel on all four sides

Horizontal nanosheets (or nanowires), stacked on top of each other
Good, much better than planar transistors
Even better, which reduces leakage and supports shorter gates and lower supply voltage
In discrete steps: the width comes from the number of fins, because fin height is fixed
Flexible: the sheet width and the number of sheets can be chosen per transistor
Fin patterning (often with SADP or SAQP), fin isolation, gate formation
Epitaxy of alternating Si and SiGe layers, selective removal of SiGe to release the sheets, inner spacers
More complex, with new steps and tighter control

when: FinFET
The workhorse of logic chips from about 22 nm to 5 nm and still used widely at 3 nm. It is mature, with well-known design rules and high yield.
GAA
The next step for the smallest nodes, where FinFETs struggle to control leakage and where designers want to tune the width of each transistor.
Beyond
Research continues on stacked complementary FETs (CFET), which place nMOS and pMOS on top of each other.
faq: Why is GAA better than FinFET?

In a gate-all-around transistor the gate surrounds the channel on all sides, which controls leakage better at very short gate lengths than a FinFET, where the gate covers three sides. It also lets designers tune the channel width of each transistor.
Are GAA transistors the same as nanosheet transistors?

Nanosheet transistors are the most common form of GAA: horizontal sheets stacked on top of each other and wrapped by the gate. Nanowire transistors are another GAA form. Intel calls its version RibbonFET and Samsung calls it MBCFET.
When did the industry move from FinFET to GAA?
FinFETs shipped in volume with Intel at 22 nm in 2012. GAA reached volume production at the 3 nm class around 2022, and other leading chipmakers followed.
What comes after GAA?
Research focuses on complementary FETs (CFET), which stack nMOS and pMOS transistors on top of each other to save area.

cpu-vs-gpu.title: CPU vs GPU: Differences in Architecture and Use
cpu-vs-gpu.description: CPU vs GPU compared in a table: design goal, core count, execution model, caches, memory bandwidth, branching, data transfer and typical workloads.
cpu-vs-gpu.lead: A CPU is built to finish one task as fast as possible, so it has a few powerful cores with large caches and smart control logic. A GPU is built to finish many similar tasks at once, so it has thousands of simple arithmetic units and hides memory delays by switching between huge numbers of threads. CPUs are good at complex, branching, serial work; GPUs are good at massively parallel math such as graphics and deep learning.
rows: Low latency: finish a single thread as fast as possible
High throughput: finish as much total work as possible
A few to a few hundred complex cores
Thousands of simple arithmetic units, grouped into larger blocks
Out-of-order execution and branch prediction in each core, plus SIMD instructions
SIMT: groups of threads (for example 32) run the same instruction together
Large caches and sophisticated control logic take much of the chip area
More area goes to arithmetic units; caches are smaller per thread
Mostly by switching to other ready threads while one waits
DDR or LPDDR, typically tens to a few hundred GB/s of bandwidth
GDDR or HBM, typically hundreds of GB/s to several TB/s of bandwidth
Handles branches and irregular code well
Slows down when threads in a group take different branches (divergence)
A discrete GPU has its own memory, so data must be copied over a bus such as PCIe
Specialized models such as CUDA, HIP, OpenCL and graphics shader languages
Operating systems, databases, control logic, general applications
Graphics, matrix and vector math, deep learning, simulation
when: CPU
When the work is serial, branchy or needs fast response from one thread: running the operating system, application logic, databases.
GPU
When the same operation is applied to a huge amount of data: rendering images, training and running neural networks, scientific simulation.
Together

Most systems use both. The CPU runs the program and prepares the data, and the GPU does the heavy parallel math. Sending too little work to a GPU can be slower than staying on the CPU, because of the cost of copying data.
faq: Why is a GPU faster than a CPU for deep learning?

Deep learning is mostly matrix math that can be split into many identical operations. A GPU has thousands of simple arithmetic units and very high memory bandwidth, so it handles this parallel work far better than the few complex cores of a CPU.
Can a GPU replace a CPU?
No. GPUs are poor at branchy, serial code and need a CPU to run the operating system and feed them data. The two work together.
What does SIMT mean on a GPU?

SIMT (single instruction, multiple threads) means a group of threads, for example 32, executes the same instruction together on different data. If threads in a group take different branches, they run one after another, which is called divergence.
Why can using a GPU be slower for small tasks?
Data must be copied between CPU memory and GPU memory over a bus such as PCIe. For a small amount of work, the copy time can be larger than the time saved by the GPU.

asic-vs-fpga-vs-soc.title: ASIC vs FPGA vs SoC: What Is the Difference?
asic-vs-fpga-vs-soc.description: ASIC vs FPGA vs SoC compared in a table: what each one is, flexibility, performance, up-front and unit cost, time to market and typical uses.
asic-vs-fpga-vs-soc.lead: These three terms describe different things. An ASIC is a chip custom-designed for one application. An FPGA is a chip whose logic you can reprogram after manufacturing. An SoC (system on chip) is a chip that integrates a whole system, such as CPU cores, a GPU, memory controllers and I/O. The terms overlap: a smartphone SoC is usually built as an ASIC, and some FPGAs include processor cores, which makes them SoCs too.
rows: A chip designed and manufactured for one specific application
A chip with programmable logic blocks and interconnect that you configure after manufacturing
A chip that integrates the main parts of a system: processor cores, memory controllers, I/O and accelerators
Hardware is fixed, but the processors run software that can be updated
Best: the logic is tailored to the task
In between: the programmable fabric costs area, speed and power
High, thanks to dedicated accelerators for common tasks
Very high: design, verification and masks can cost millions to hundreds of millions of dollars at advanced nodes
Low: you buy a ready-made device
High, similar to an ASIC, because it is a custom chip
Long: design, verification and fabrication take many months to years
Short: a design can be running in days or weeks
Expensive: usually needs a new set of masks (a respin)
Expensive, though some problems can be worked around in software
Cryptocurrency miners, network and storage controllers, dedicated codecs
Prototyping, low-volume products, telecom and test equipment, hardware acceleration
Smartphones, tablets, game consoles and many embedded devices
when: ASIC
When the volume is high, the function is stable and you need the best performance and power efficiency per unit cost.
FPGA
When the volume is low, the requirements may change, or you need to start quickly: prototypes, early products, specialized equipment.
SoC
When you want a complete product in one chip, such as a phone. In practice an SoC is designed as an ASIC, and FPGAs are often used to prototype it before manufacturing.
faq: Is an SoC an ASIC?

In practice, usually yes. SoC describes what is integrated on the chip (a whole system), while ASIC describes how it is designed (custom for an application). A smartphone SoC is normally built as an ASIC.
Why are FPGAs used to prototype ASICs?
An FPGA can be reprogrammed in hours, so designers can test and fix their logic before paying for expensive masks. A bug found in an ASIC after manufacturing usually requires a respin.
When is an ASIC cheaper than an FPGA?
At high volume. An ASIC has a very high up-front cost but the lowest cost per unit, while an FPGA has a low up-front cost but a higher price per unit.
Are FPGAs slower than ASICs?
Generally yes. The programmable fabric costs area, speed and power, so a custom ASIC doing the same job is faster and more power-efficient.

sic-vs-gan.title: SiC vs GaN Power Devices: Key Differences
sic-vs-gan.description: SiC vs GaN power semiconductors compared in a table: band gap, thermal conductivity, device type, voltage range, switching frequency, wafers, cost and uses.
sic-vs-gan.lead: Silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) are both wide-bandgap semiconductors that beat silicon in power conversion: they withstand higher fields, switch faster and lose less energy. The practical split is voltage. SiC is the choice for high-voltage, high-power systems such as electric-vehicle inverters, while GaN excels at lower voltages and very high switching frequencies, such as compact fast chargers.
rows: About 3.3 eV (4H-SiC), compared with 1.12 eV for silicon
About ten times that of silicon
About ten times that of silicon
High, roughly three times silicon, which makes cooling easier
Similar to silicon, lower than SiC
Lateral HEMTs that use a two-dimensional electron gas as the channel
Around 650 V to 3.3 kV, and higher
Very high (hundreds of kHz up to MHz)
SiC wafers are expensive and difficult to grow
Usually grown on silicon wafers (GaN-on-Si), which is cheaper and works in silicon fabs; GaN-on-SiC is used for RF
Gate oxide reliability and the need for higher gate drive voltage
Normally-on behavior must be avoided, and the gate tolerates only a small voltage swing
EV traction inverters, on-board chargers, solar inverters, industrial motor drives, railways
Compact fast chargers and adapters, data-center power supplies, 5G RF amplifiers
when: SiC
When voltage and power are high and efficiency and heat matter: vehicle inverters, solar and industrial power systems.
GaN
When voltage is moderate and you want small, light, very efficient converters at high switching frequency: chargers, adapters, server power.
Either
Both need care at high switching speed, because fast edges cause ringing and noise. Layout and gate driving matter as much as the device.
faq: Which is better, SiC or GaN?
Neither is better overall. SiC suits high voltage and power, such as electric-vehicle inverters, while GaN suits lower voltage and very high switching frequency, such as compact chargers.
Why are SiC and GaN better than silicon for power devices?
Both have a wider band gap and about ten times the critical electric field of silicon, so they withstand higher voltages, switch faster and lose less energy.
Why is GaN-on-silicon cheaper than SiC?
GaN power devices are usually grown on silicon wafers, which are cheap and fit existing silicon fabs. SiC wafers are expensive and hard to grow.
Which handles heat better, SiC or GaN?
SiC. Its thermal conductivity is roughly three times that of silicon, while GaN is similar to silicon.

euv-vs-duv.title: EUV vs DUV Lithography: What Is the Difference?
euv-vs-duv.description: EUV vs DUV (ArF immersion) lithography compared in a table: wavelength, light source, optics, masks, resolution, cost, defects and where each is used.
euv-vs-duv.lead: Lithography prints circuit patterns on the wafer with light. DUV (deep ultraviolet) lithography uses 193 nm light from an ArF laser, with lenses and a layer of water between the lens and wafer (immersion). EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography uses 13.5 nm light, so it can print far finer patterns in a single exposure, but the light is absorbed by almost everything, so the whole system must be built from mirrors in a vacuum. EUV is far more expensive and complex.

Lenses (refractive), with water between the last lens and the wafer in immersion systems
Only mirrors (reflective multilayers), because almost every material absorbs EUV light
Reflective mask with a multilayer coating
Air or nitrogen, plus the immersion water
Single exposure resolves pitches down to about 80 nm; finer patterns need multiple patterning
Single exposure can print pitches around 30 nm or below; High-NA EUV goes further
Multiple patterning (such as SADP, SAQP) multiplies the number of steps
Fewer steps for the finest layers, but new challenges in resists and masks
Overlay errors and defects from multiple patterning
Stochastic defects caused by the small number of photons, and mask defects
Tens of millions of dollars per tool
Well over a hundred million dollars per tool
ASML is effectively the only supplier
Most layers of most chips, including advanced ones
The most critical, finest layers at roughly the 7 nm class and below
when: DUV
Still prints the large majority of layers, even in leading-edge chips. It is mature, fast and much cheaper per layer.
EUV
Used for the finest critical layers, where DUV would need several patterning steps. It simplifies the process but the tools and operating costs are very high.
Next
High-NA EUV uses a larger numerical aperture to resolve even smaller features for the next nodes.
faq: Why does EUV use a 13.5 nm wavelength?

A shorter wavelength prints finer patterns. At 13.5 nm, EUV light is about 14 times shorter than the 193 nm light of ArF DUV, so a single exposure can print features that would need multiple patterning with DUV.
Why are EUV systems so expensive?
The light source is a laser-heated tin plasma, the optics are all multilayer mirrors, and the whole system runs in a vacuum. A single tool costs well over a hundred million dollars.
Who makes EUV lithography machines?
ASML is effectively the only supplier of EUV lithography tools.
Has EUV replaced DUV?
No. Most layers, even in advanced chips, are still printed with DUV. EUV is used for the finest, most critical layers.

cmos-vs-ccd-image-sensor.title: CMOS vs CCD Image Sensors: Differences Explained
cmos-vs-ccd-image-sensor.description: CMOS vs CCD image sensors compared in a table: readout method, power, speed, noise, shutter type, integration, cost and typical uses.
cmos-vs-ccd-image-sensor.lead: Both sensors turn light into electric charge in each pixel; they differ in how that charge is read out. A CCD moves the charge pixel by pixel to a single output amplifier. A CMOS sensor converts charge to voltage inside each pixel and reads many pixels in parallel. CMOS sensors are cheaper, faster and use less power, and they can integrate ADCs and image processing on the same chip, so they have replaced CCDs in almost all consumer products.

Standard CMOS-type process, built in common semiconductor fabs
Special process designed for charge transfer
ADCs, timing and image processing can be integrated; stacked designs add logic and memory
Mostly only the sensor; supporting circuits are separate chips
High, because charge transfer needs high-speed clocks and several supply voltages
Lower, limited by the serial transfer
Once worse, now comparable or better thanks to pinned photodiodes and correlated double sampling
Traditionally low noise and uniform pixels
Rolling shutter is common (fast subjects can look skewed); global shutter versions need extra pixel circuitry

Smartphones, digital cameras, automotive cameras, webcams
Scientific and astronomical cameras, some industrial, medical and space imaging
when: CMOS
Almost everything today: phones, cameras, cars, security and industrial cameras. It is cheap, fast and flexible, with backside-illuminated and stacked versions improving sensitivity and speed.
CCD
Special cases that value its long track record of low noise and uniformity, such as some scientific, astronomy and space instruments.
faq: Why did CMOS sensors replace CCDs?
CMOS sensors are cheaper, faster and use less power, and they can integrate ADCs and image processing on the same chip. Improvements in noise and sensitivity removed the main advantage of the CCD.
What is a rolling shutter?
A rolling shutter reads the rows of a CMOS sensor one after another, so fast-moving subjects look skewed. A global shutter exposes all pixels at once but needs extra circuitry in each pixel.
Is CCD still used?
Yes, in some scientific, astronomical, industrial and space imaging where its long record of low noise and uniformity matters.
What is blooming?
Blooming happens when a bright pixel overflows and spills charge into neighboring pixels. CCDs are more prone to it than CMOS sensors.

wet-vs-dry-etching.title: Wet vs Dry Etching: Key Differences in Semiconductor Processing
wet-vs-dry-etching.description: Wet vs dry etching compared in a table: medium, directionality, selectivity, resolution, throughput, damage, cost and where each is used in chip manufacturing.
wet-vs-dry-etching.lead: Etching removes material from the wafer to form patterns. Wet etching dissolves the material in a liquid chemical; it is simple, fast and highly selective, but it usually etches sideways as well as down (isotropic). Dry etching uses a plasma of reactive gases in a vacuum chamber, and ions can make it strongly directional (anisotropic), which is essential for cutting narrow, vertical features in modern chips.

Lower, and tuned by gas chemistry and plasma conditions
Limited by undercut; used for larger features and film removal

Lower: usually one wafer at a time

when: Wet etching
When selectivity matters more than shape, or when you are removing a whole film or cleaning: stripping oxide, removing nitride, MEMS bulk etching.
Dry etching
When the pattern is fine and you need vertical walls: transistor gates, contacts, trenches and vias.
Together
A chip flow uses both. Dry etching defines the fine patterns, and wet steps clean and strip films afterwards.
faq: What is the difference between isotropic and anisotropic etching?

Isotropic etching removes material equally in all directions, so it undercuts the mask. Anisotropic etching removes it mainly in one direction (down), leaving vertical sidewalls. Wet etching is usually isotropic, while dry etching can be anisotropic.
Why is dry etching used for fine patterns?
Ions in the plasma give dry etching a strong direction, so narrow, vertical features can be cut. Wet etching undercuts the mask and cannot make nanometer-scale patterns.
Why is wet etching still used?
It is simple, fast, processes many wafers at once and has very high selectivity. It is used for cleaning, stripping films and bulk silicon etching in MEMS.
What is selectivity in etching?

Selectivity is how much faster the target material etches than the material you want to keep. Wet etching usually has very high selectivity, while dry etching is tuned through gas chemistry and plasma conditions.

risc-vs-cisc.title: RISC vs CISC: Differences and Examples
risc-vs-cisc.description: RISC vs CISC instruction set architectures compared in a table: instruction length, memory access, registers, decoding, code size, examples such as ARM, RISC-V and x86.
risc-vs-cisc.lead: RISC (reduced instruction set computer) and CISC (complex instruction set computer) are two philosophies for designing an instruction set. RISC uses a small set of simple, fixed-length instructions that are easy to pipeline. CISC uses a larger set of complex, variable-length instructions that can do more work per instruction. Today the line is blurred: modern x86 processors translate CISC instructions into simpler internal operations, so the difference now matters mostly at the level of the instruction set and software ecosystem.

A large set of powerful instructions, some doing several steps at once
