Variable (x86 instructions are 1 to 15 bytes long)
Load/store architecture: only load and store instructions touch memory; arithmetic works on registers
Many instructions can use memory operands directly
Many general-purpose registers (32 in RISC-V and AArch64)
Simple, which helps pipelining and keeps the hardware small
Complex; modern x86 cores translate instructions into internal micro-operations
Larger, though compressed instruction extensions (such as Thumb or RISC-V C) reduce it
Often denser, because one instruction does more
x86 and x86-64 (Intel, AMD), IBM z/Architecture
Smartphones, embedded systems, and increasingly laptops and servers
PCs and servers, where software compatibility is essential
when: RISC
A good fit when power efficiency and a simple, scalable design matter: phones, embedded devices, custom processors. RISC-V is an open standard, so anyone can build a core without license fees.
CISC
The reason to use it today is software compatibility: the huge existing x86 software base keeps it dominant in PCs and servers.
In practice
Performance depends more on the microarchitecture, caches and manufacturing process than on whether an instruction set is called RISC or CISC.
faq: Is ARM RISC or CISC?
ARM is a RISC architecture. RISC-V is also RISC, while x86 is CISC.
Is RISC faster than CISC?

Not by itself. Modern x86 processors translate CISC instructions into simpler internal operations, so performance depends more on the microarchitecture, caches and manufacturing process than on the label.
Why does x86 still dominate PCs?
Compatibility. The huge amount of existing Windows and desktop software is built for x86, which keeps it dominant in PCs and servers.
What is a load/store architecture?
In a load/store architecture only load and store instructions access memory, and arithmetic works on registers. RISC designs such as ARM and RISC-V work this way.

i2c-vs-spi-vs-uart.title: I2C vs SPI vs UART: Differences and When to Use Each
i2c-vs-spi-vs-uart.description: I2C vs SPI vs UART compared in a table: number of wires, clock, speed, topology, addressing, error checking and typical uses in microcontroller projects.
i2c-vs-spi-vs-uart.lead: These are the three serial interfaces you meet first in embedded systems. UART is a simple point-to-point link with no shared clock. SPI is a fast, four-wire bus where one master selects each device with a chip-select line. I2C is a two-wire bus where many devices share the same lines and are picked by address. The trade-off is mostly between speed (SPI), pin count (I2C) and simplicity (UART).
rows: Two signal wires (TX and RX) plus ground
Four signal wires (SCLK, MOSI, MISO) plus one chip-select (CS) per device
Two shared wires (SDA and SCL) plus ground, with pull-up resistors
Asynchronous: no clock line, so both sides must agree on the baud rate
Synchronous: the master drives a clock
Synchronous: the master drives a clock
Point to point between two devices
One master and several slaves, each slave needing its own CS line
Several masters and slaves share one bus
7-bit address (10-bit optional) sent at the start of each transfer
From 9,600 to 115,200 bit/s up to a few Mbit/s
Often 1 to 50 MHz, and higher on some parts
Optional parity bit and framing check
Two more pins for every additional link
One more CS pin for every additional device
Can run longer with RS-232 or RS-485 drivers
Debug console, GPS and Bluetooth modules, board-to-board links
Flash memory, SD cards, displays, fast ADCs and sensors
Low-speed sensors, EEPROM, real-time clocks, chip configuration
when: UART
When you need the simplest possible link between two devices, a debug console or a module with a serial interface.
SPI
When you need speed: memory, displays, fast converters. The price is more pins as you add devices.
I2C
When you have many slow devices and few pins: sensors, small memories, configuration registers. Speed is limited and pull-up resistors are required.
faq: Which is faster, I2C or SPI?
SPI. It often runs at 1 to 50 MHz or more, while I2C runs at 100 kHz to 1 MHz in common modes, and 3.4 MHz in high-speed mode.
Why does I2C need pull-up resistors?
I2C devices only pull the lines low and release them to go high, so resistors pull the lines up. This lets many devices share two wires safely.
Do UART devices need a clock line?
No. UART is asynchronous, so both sides must be set to the same baud rate. A small baud-rate mismatch can garble characters.
How many pins does SPI need for many devices?
SPI needs shared SCLK, MOSI and MISO lines plus one chip-select pin per device, so the pin count grows with the number of devices. I2C needs only two pins regardless of the number of devices.

slc-vs-mlc-vs-tlc-vs-qlc.title: SLC vs MLC vs TLC vs QLC NAND: Differences Explained
slc-vs-mlc-vs-tlc-vs-qlc.description: SLC vs MLC vs TLC vs QLC NAND flash compared in a table: bits per cell, endurance, speed, cost, error rate and which SSDs use each type.
slc-vs-mlc-vs-tlc-vs-qlc.lead: The name tells you how many bits one NAND flash cell stores: one (SLC), two (MLC), three (TLC) or four (QLC). Storing more bits per cell packs more capacity into the same silicon and lowers the cost per bit, but the cell must distinguish more voltage levels that sit closer together. So endurance, speed and reliability all get worse as you go from SLC to QLC.
rows: Highest, the strongest ECC and read-retry needed
Capacity for the same die area
Industrial and aerospace storage, enterprise write caches
Older enterprise and high-end consumer SSDs
Mainstream consumer SSDs, phones, memory cards
Large, low-cost drives and read-heavy storage
when: SLC
When endurance and reliability matter more than price: industrial systems, logging, and the fast cache area of other SSDs.
TLC
The mainstream choice today, balancing cost, speed and endurance for PCs and phones.
QLC
When capacity per dollar matters and the workload is mostly reading: bulk storage, game libraries, archives.
Mixed
Many TLC and QLC SSDs use part of the space as a fast SLC-mode cache to absorb bursts of writes. When that cache is full, write speed drops.
faq: Which is better, TLC or QLC?
TLC is faster and has higher endurance, so it is the mainstream choice. QLC is cheaper per gigabyte and suits read-heavy storage, but it wears out faster.
Why does endurance drop as bits per cell increase?
More bits per cell means more threshold voltage levels packed closer together, so the widening of those levels caused by wear leads to read errors sooner.
What is an SLC cache?
Many TLC and QLC SSDs use part of their space in fast SLC mode to absorb bursts of writes. When that cache is full, the write speed drops.
How many voltage levels must QLC distinguish?
Sixteen, compared with 2 for SLC, 4 for MLC and 8 for TLC.

ddr-vs-lpddr-vs-gddr-vs-hbm.title: DDR vs LPDDR vs GDDR vs HBM: DRAM Types Compared
ddr-vs-lpddr-vs-gddr-vs-hbm.description: DDR vs LPDDR vs GDDR vs HBM compared in a table: target devices, bus width, speed, bandwidth, power, packaging, capacity and cost.
ddr-vs-lpddr-vs-gddr-vs-hbm.lead: All four are DRAM, but they are tuned for different jobs. DDR is the standard main memory for PCs and servers. LPDDR cuts power for phones and thin laptops. GDDR pushes per-pin speed for graphics cards. HBM stacks dies and uses a very wide bus, giving the highest bandwidth for AI accelerators at the highest cost.
rows: 64 bits per channel on a DIMM (DDR5 splits this into two 32-bit halves)
32 bits per chip, with many chips around the GPU
Moderate to high (LPDDR5X reaches 8,533 MT/s and beyond)
Very high (GDDR6X over 20 Gb/s, GDDR7 around 30 Gb/s)
Lower per pin, because the bus is so wide
Tens of GB/s per device or package
Tens to a hundred GB/s per chip, several hundred GB/s to over 1 TB/s per card
Hundreds of GB/s per stack, several TB/s per accelerator
Lowest per bit: low voltage and deep power-down modes
Efficient per bit, but stacked dies are hard to cool
Memory modules (DIMMs) in sockets, or soldered
Soldered, or stacked on the processor package (PoP)
Soldered on the graphics board around the GPU
Stacked dies joined by TSVs, placed next to the processor on a silicon interposer
Highest: from several GB to hundreds of GB per module
Several GB to tens of GB
Highest, because of stacking and advanced packaging
when: DDR
General-purpose main memory where large capacity, low cost and upgradability matter.
LPDDR
Battery-powered devices, where energy per bit and size matter more than capacity.
GDDR
Graphics and gaming, where high bandwidth is needed at a reasonable price.
HBM
AI training and high-performance computing, where bandwidth is the bottleneck and cost is secondary.
faq: Why do GPUs use GDDR or HBM instead of DDR?

GPUs move huge amounts of data, so they need far more bandwidth than DDR provides. GDDR raises the speed of each pin, while HBM uses a very wide bus, 1,024 bits per stack, right next to the processor.
Is LPDDR the same as DDR?

They share the same basic technology, but LPDDR is tuned for low power with a lower voltage and deep power-down modes. It is usually soldered or stacked on the processor, so it cannot be upgraded later.
Why is HBM so expensive?
HBM stacks several DRAM dies connected by TSVs and must be placed on a silicon interposer next to the processor. The stacking and advanced packaging add cost and make cooling harder.
Can I upgrade LPDDR, GDDR or HBM memory?
No. Unlike DDR modules (DIMMs), they are soldered to the board or built into the package.

mram-vs-reram-vs-pcm-vs-feram.title: MRAM vs ReRAM vs PCM vs FeRAM: Emerging Memories Compared
mram-vs-reram-vs-pcm-vs-feram.description: MRAM, ReRAM, PCM and FeRAM compared in a table: storage principle, write method, speed, endurance, density, main challenges and typical uses.
mram-vs-reram-vs-pcm-vs-feram.lead: These four emerging non-volatile memories all try to combine the speed of RAM with data retention without power. They differ in what stores the bit: the magnetization of a thin film (MRAM), the resistance of a filament in an oxide (ReRAM), the crystalline or amorphous state of a material (PCM) or the polarization of a ferroelectric (FeRAM). None has replaced DRAM or flash broadly yet, but each has found a niche.
rows: Magnetization direction of a free layer in a magnetic tunnel junction, read as low or high resistance
Resistance of a conductive filament that forms and breaks in a metal-oxide layer
Crystalline (low resistance) or amorphous (high resistance) state of a phase-change material
Polarization direction of a ferroelectric material in a capacitor
Spin-transfer torque (STT) or spin-orbit torque (SOT) current
Heat pulses: melt and quench to make it amorphous, anneal to crystallize
An electric field flips the polarization
Capacitor type: destructive, so the data must be rewritten after reading
Fast: writes in a few to tens of ns
Fast to moderate (tens of ns to microseconds)
Fast reads; writes slower and need more energy
Moderate to high, varies by design
Moderate: larger cells, hard to stack
High potential: simple cells, crossbar arrays
Lower: the capacitor is hard to shrink
Write energy, cell size and process complexity
Variability between cells, the initial forming step
High write current, resistance drift over time
Scaling the capacitor, integrating ferroelectric materials
Embedded memory in microcontrollers and automotive devices, data logging
Embedded non-volatile memory, in-memory computing for AI
Small low-power memory in smart cards, meters and IoT devices
when: MRAM
When you need non-volatile memory with flash-like retention but DRAM-like speed and almost unlimited endurance, for example embedded memory or frequent logging.
ReRAM
When you want a simple, dense, low-voltage cell, including for in-memory computing that does multiply-accumulate in the memory array.
PCM
When you want a denser memory between DRAM and flash, and can accept higher write energy.
FeRAM
When you need very low-power, fast, high-endurance memory in small amounts, such as smart cards and sensors.
faq: Which emerging memory is closest to replacing DRAM or SRAM?

MRAM comes closest in speed and endurance, with writes in a few to tens of nanoseconds and over 10¹⁰ cycles. But its larger cells keep it far behind DRAM and flash in capacity and cost per bit, so it is used as embedded memory.
How does phase-change memory store data?
It heats a material to switch it between a crystalline, low-resistance state and an amorphous, high-resistance state. The resistance is then read as 0 or 1.
Why is the read in capacitor-type FeRAM destructive?
Reading flips the polarization to sense it, which erases the stored value, so the data must be written back after each read.
What is in-memory computing with ReRAM?
A ReRAM array can perform multiply-accumulate operations directly in the memory by using each cell resistance as a weight. This suits AI workloads and avoids moving data between memory and processor.

verilog-vs-vhdl.title: Verilog vs VHDL: Differences Between the Two HDLs
verilog-vs-vhdl.description: Verilog vs VHDL compared in a table: origin, syntax, typing, case sensitivity, verification features, who uses each and how to choose.
verilog-vs-vhdl.lead: Verilog and VHDL are the two main hardware description languages (HDLs) used to describe digital circuits for simulation and synthesis. Verilog has short, C-like syntax and is easier to start with. VHDL is verbose and strongly typed, which catches more mistakes early. Both can describe the same circuits, and the choice usually depends on the industry, the company and the existing code.
rows: Created in the 1980s at Gateway Design Automation and standardized as IEEE 1364
Developed for the US Department of Defense and standardized as IEEE 1076 in 1987
Weakly typed: implicit conversions are easy but can hide mistakes
Strongly typed: explicit conversions are needed, so errors are caught at compile time
Verilog alone is limited; SystemVerilog adds classes, constrained-random tests, assertions and UVM
VHDL-2008 plus libraries such as OSVVM and UVVM
Richer: packages, generics, records and enumerated types
Supported by all major simulators and synthesis tools
Supported by all major simulators and synthesis tools, and mixed-language simulation is possible
ASIC and SoC design, especially in the US and Asia
Europe, aerospace and defense, and many FPGA projects
when: Verilog / SystemVerilog
A good default for chip design and verification, because the industry tools and libraries are built around SystemVerilog.
VHDL
A good choice where strict typing and long-term maintainability matter, such as safety-critical and defense projects.
In practice
You often need to read both. The ideas (modules or entities, concurrent signals, clocked processes) are the same.
faq: Which is easier to learn, Verilog or VHDL?
Verilog, because its syntax is short and C-like. VHDL is more verbose and strongly typed, which is harder at first but catches more mistakes at compile time.
Which is more used in industry?
SystemVerilog dominates ASIC and SoC design and verification, especially in the US and Asia. VHDL is common in Europe, aerospace and defense, and many FPGA projects.
Can Verilog and VHDL be mixed in one project?
Yes. Major simulators and synthesis tools support mixed-language designs, so a module written in one language can be used in the other.
What is SystemVerilog?
SystemVerilog is an extension of Verilog that adds classes, constrained-random testing, assertions and the UVM methodology, which makes it the standard for chip verification.

nvme-vs-sata-ssd.title: NVMe vs SATA SSD: Speed, Interface and Which to Buy
nvme-vs-sata-ssd.description: NVMe vs SATA SSD compared in a table: interface, speed, latency, command queues, form factor, power, compatibility, cost and who each is best for.
nvme-vs-sata-ssd.lead: Both are SSDs with flash memory inside, but they connect to the computer differently. A SATA SSD uses the SATA interface, designed for hard disks, which tops out at about 550 MB/s. An NVMe SSD talks over PCI Express with a protocol built for flash, reaching 3 to 14 GB/s or more with lower latency. For everyday use the difference is small, but for large file transfers and heavy workloads NVMe is far faster.
rows: About 3.5 GB/s (PCIe 3.0 x4), 7 GB/s (PCIe 4.0 x4) and 14 GB/s (PCIe 5.0 x4)
Up to 65,535 queues of up to 65,536 commands each
M.2, U.2 or U.3, and add-in cards
Higher at peak speed; fast drives often need a heatsink to avoid throttling
Works in very old PCs and in 2.5-inch bays
Needs an M.2 or PCIe slot and firmware that can boot from NVMe
Cheap, and similar to entry-level NVMe
Slightly more for the fastest drives; entry-level NVMe is now close to SATA prices
Upgrading older PCs and laptops, bulk storage
Modern PCs, gaming, video editing, workstations and servers
when: SATA SSD
When your computer has no NVMe slot, or when you just want a cheap, simple upgrade from a hard disk.
NVMe SSD
When you have an M.2 slot, move large files often, or need low latency: it is the default choice for new systems.
Check first
An M.2 slot can be SATA, NVMe or both. Check the manual before you buy, because an M.2 SATA drive and an M.2 NVMe drive look similar.
faq: Is NVMe much faster than SATA?
For sequential transfers, yes. SATA tops out at about 550 MB/s, while NVMe over PCIe 4.0 x4 reaches about 7 GB/s. In everyday tasks the difference feels smaller.
Can I use an NVMe SSD in any M.2 slot?
No. An M.2 slot can be SATA, NVMe or both, and the drives look similar. Check the manual of your motherboard or laptop before buying.
Do NVMe SSDs get hot?
Fast ones can, because they draw more power at peak speed, and many need a heatsink to avoid throttling. SATA SSDs run cooler.
Why does NVMe have lower latency?
NVMe was designed for flash memory. It talks over PCIe and supports up to 65,535 command queues of up to 65,536 commands each, while the AHCI protocol of SATA has a single queue of 32 commands.

mcu-vs-mpu.title: MCU vs MPU: Microcontroller vs Microprocessor Compared
mcu-vs-mpu.description: MCU vs MPU compared in a table: integration, clock speed, memory, operating system, real-time behavior, power, boot time, cost and typical uses.
mcu-vs-mpu.lead: A microcontroller (MCU) puts a processor, flash memory, RAM and peripherals such as timers, ADCs and communication interfaces on one chip, so it can run a complete small system by itself. A microprocessor (MPU) is mainly a faster processor that needs external DRAM and storage, and usually runs a full operating system such as Linux. MCUs suit simple, low-power, real-time control; MPUs suit complex, software-rich devices.
rows: CPU, flash, RAM and peripherals (GPIO, timers, ADC, UART, SPI, I2C) on one chip
CPU cores with caches and an MMU; DRAM and storage are external chips
About 1 MHz to a few hundred MHz
Hundreds of MHz to several GHz
Kilobytes to a few megabytes of on-chip flash, and kilobytes to megabytes of SRAM
External DRAM (hundreds of MB to GB) and storage such as eMMC or SD
Bare-metal code or a small real-time OS (such as FreeRTOS or Zephyr)
A full operating system such as Linux or Android
Predictable, with interrupt latency of microseconds
Harder to guarantee on Linux without real-time extensions
Very low: microamps in sleep, and a coin cell can last years
Higher: hundreds of milliwatts to watts
Seconds, because a boot loader and OS must start
Cheap chip, simple board, few external parts
More expensive chip plus DRAM and power chips, and a complex multilayer board
Appliances, motor control, sensors, wearables, automotive ECUs
Smartphones, tablets, set-top boxes, routers, industrial touchscreens, infotainment
Application processors such as NXP i.MX, TI Sitara and the chip in Raspberry Pi
when: MCU
When the job is control and sensing, you need very low power and instant start, and the program fits in on-chip memory.
MPU
When you need a rich user interface, networking, a file system or large software stacks that rely on an operating system.
Both
Many products combine them: an MPU runs the user interface and applications, while an MCU handles time-critical control and power management.
faq: What is the difference between a microcontroller and a microprocessor?

A microcontroller integrates a CPU, flash, RAM and peripherals on one chip and runs a small system by itself. A microprocessor is mainly the CPU, needs external DRAM and storage, and usually runs an operating system such as Linux.
Is the Raspberry Pi a microcontroller?
No. The Raspberry Pi uses a microprocessor-class chip with external memory and runs Linux. The Raspberry Pi Pico is a microcontroller board.
Which uses less power?
A microcontroller. It can sleep at microamps and run for years on a coin cell, while a microprocessor draws hundreds of milliwatts to watts.
Can a microcontroller run Linux?
Generally no, because Linux needs an MMU and much more memory than a typical MCU has. Microcontrollers usually run bare-metal code or a small real-time operating system.

process-vs-thread.title: Process vs Thread: Differences Explained
process-vs-thread.description: Process vs thread compared in a table: memory, creation cost, context switching, communication, isolation, synchronization and typical uses.
process-vs-thread.lead: A process is a running program with its own private address space and resources. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process. All the threads of one process share its memory, which makes them cheap to create and fast to communicate, but also means that one bug or crash can affect the whole process. Separate processes are isolated from each other, which is safer but costs more to create and to talk across.
rows: A running program with its own address space, files and other resources
A path of execution inside a process, with its own stack and registers
Separate virtual address space, isolated from other processes
Shares the code, heap and global data of its process; only the stack is private
Heavier: a new address space must be set up (copy-on-write reduces the cost)
More expensive: the address space changes, and cached translations (TLB) may be lost
Cheaper: the address space and caches stay the same
Needs inter-process communication such as pipes, sockets or shared memory
Reads and writes shared memory directly, which is fast
A crash usually stays inside the process
A crash in one thread can bring down the whole process
Needed when processes share memory or files
Always needed for shared data: mutexes and atomics, or the program has data races and deadlocks
The unit that the operating system actually schedules onto CPU cores
Isolation and security: browser tabs, services, shell pipelines
Parallel work inside one program: servers handling many connections, background tasks, parallel computation
when: Process
When you want isolation, robustness or security, or when pieces of software are written by different parties and should not share memory.
Thread
When tasks need to share data quickly and you want to use several CPU cores inside one program.
Care needed
Threads sharing memory is both their strength and their danger. Protect shared data with locks or atomic operations, and watch out for deadlock.
faq: Do threads share memory?
Yes. Threads in one process share its code, heap and global data. Each thread has its own stack and registers.
Why are threads cheaper to create than processes?
A new process needs its own address space, while a thread reuses that of its process. Switching between threads also avoids changing the address space, so it costs less.
What happens if one thread crashes?
It can bring down the whole process, because the threads share memory. A crash in one process usually does not affect other processes.
When should I use processes instead of threads?
When you want isolation and robustness, such as browser tabs or independent services, or when different parts should not be able to corrupt the memory of the other parts.

cvd-vs-pvd.title: CVD vs PVD: Thin-Film Deposition Compared
cvd-vs-pvd.description: CVD vs PVD compared in a table: principle, typical materials, step coverage, temperature, purity, environment, hazards and where each is used in chip making.
cvd-vs-pvd.lead: Both methods deposit thin films on wafers. In chemical vapor deposition (CVD), gases react on the wafer surface to form the film. In physical vapor deposition (PVD), such as sputtering, atoms are knocked out of a solid target and land on the wafer without a chemical reaction. CVD is the usual choice for insulators and for coating deep structures evenly; PVD is the usual choice for metals.
rows: Gaseous precursors react chemically on the heated or plasma-activated wafer surface
Atoms are ejected physically from a solid target (for example by argon ions) and condense on the wafer
Silicon dioxide, silicon nitride, polysilicon, tungsten, low-k dielectrics
Metals such as aluminum, titanium, titanium nitride, tantalum and copper seed layers
Good, especially for LPCVD; ALD is even better
Line-of-sight deposition, so deep trenches and holes are covered poorly (improved by ionized PVD)
Higher: LPCVD at about 600 to 800 °C, plasma CVD at about 200 to 400 °C
Lower: from room temperature to a few hundred degrees
Can include hydrogen, carbon or chlorine left over from the precursors
High, set by the purity of the target
Atmospheric to low pressure, with reactive gases
High vacuum with an inert gas plasma
Toxic, flammable or corrosive gases (silane, WF6) need careful handling and abatement
Fewer hazardous chemicals, but high vacuum and plasma systems
Interlayer dielectrics, spacers, polysilicon gates, tungsten plugs
Barrier and seed layers for copper wiring, aluminum pads, contact metals
when: CVD
When you need an insulating film, or a film that must coat steep features evenly.
PVD
When you need a pure metal film at low temperature, for example the seed layer for copper plating.
Together
A chip uses both: CVD builds the insulating layers, and PVD deposits the thin metal liners inside the openings before they are filled.
faq: What is the main difference between CVD and PVD?
CVD forms the film by chemical reactions of gases on the wafer, while PVD, such as sputtering, physically ejects atoms from a solid target onto the wafer.
Why is CVD better at coating steep structures?
Gas molecules can reach into trenches and holes and react everywhere on the surface. PVD deposits in straight lines, so deep, narrow features are covered poorly.
Which is used for metal wiring?
Both. PVD is used for barrier and seed layers and aluminum pads, while CVD deposits tungsten plugs. Copper is filled by electroplating over a PVD seed layer.
What is PECVD?
Plasma-enhanced CVD uses a plasma to activate the gases, so films can be deposited at lower temperatures, around 200 to 400 °C.

ald-vs-cvd.title: ALD vs CVD: Atomic Layer Deposition Compared
ald-vs-cvd.description: ALD vs CVD compared in a table: how each works, thickness control, conformality, speed, temperature, uniformity and typical uses in advanced chips.
ald-vs-cvd.lead: ALD (atomic layer deposition) is a special form of CVD in which the precursor gases are pulsed in one at a time, and each pulse reacts only until the surface is covered. The film therefore grows one atomic layer per cycle, with perfect control of thickness and excellent coverage of very deep structures. The price is speed: ALD is much slower than ordinary CVD, so it is used for the thinnest and most critical films.
rows: Precursors are pulsed in turn, separated by purges. Each reaction is self-limiting, so one cycle adds about one atomic layer
Precursors flow in together and react continuously on the surface
Atomic-level, set by the number of cycles
Set by deposition time and rate, so less precise
Excellent, even in very deep, narrow holes and trenches
Good, but deep structures can pinch off before they are filled
Slow: a fraction of a nanometer per cycle
Fast: many nanometers per minute or more
Very uniform, dense and with few pinholes
Wide range, often higher (plasma CVD is lower)
High-k gate dielectrics (such as HfO2), thin barriers, spacers, liners in 3D structures
Thick insulating films, polysilicon, silicon nitride, tungsten plugs
when: ALD
When the film must be extremely thin, perfectly uniform and must coat complex 3D structures: gate stacks of FinFETs and GAA transistors, DRAM capacitors.
CVD
When you need thicker films quickly and at lower cost, and the structure is not too demanding.
Trade-off
Engineers often combine them: ALD for the first thin conformal layer, then faster CVD to fill or thicken.
faq: Why is ALD slow?

Each cycle adds only about one atomic layer, because the precursors are pulsed one at a time with purges in between. That gives perfect thickness control but a rate of a fraction of a nanometer per cycle.
Why is ALD used for gate dielectrics?
High-k gate dielectrics such as HfO2 must be only a few nanometers thick, perfectly uniform and must coat 3D structures such as fins evenly. ALD does all three.
Is ALD a type of CVD?
Yes. ALD can be seen as a special form of CVD in which the reactions are separated in time and are self-limiting.
When is CVD preferred over ALD?
When a thicker film is needed quickly and cheaply and the structure is not too demanding, such as thick insulating films.

thermal-diffusion-vs-ion-implantation.title: Thermal Diffusion vs Ion Implantation: Doping Methods Compared
thermal-diffusion-vs-ion-implantation.description: Thermal diffusion vs ion implantation compared in a table: principle, dose control, depth profile, temperature, crystal damage, cost and typical uses.
thermal-diffusion-vs-ion-implantation.lead: Both methods put dopant atoms into silicon to control its electrical behavior. In thermal diffusion, dopants move in from a source at high temperature. In ion implantation, dopant ions are accelerated and shot into the wafer. Implantation gives far better control over how much dopant goes in and where, so it replaced diffusion for almost all doping in modern ICs, although it needs an annealing step to repair the crystal.
rows: Dopant atoms diffuse into hot silicon (about 900 to 1,100 °C) from a gas, solid or film source, driven by the concentration gradient
Dopant ions are accelerated by an electric field (keV to MeV) and shot into the wafer
Harder: depends on surface concentration, temperature and time
Precise: the dose is measured as ion current
Highest concentration at the surface, falling with depth
Peak below the surface at a depth set by the ion energy
Isotropic: also spreads sideways under the mask
Almost directional; a photoresist mask is enough
Near room temperature during implantation, but annealing at high temperature is needed afterwards
Damages the lattice; annealing repairs it and activates the dopants
Well suited: low energy places dopants near the surface
High: an ion implanter is a large, expensive tool
Drive-in of deep wells, solar-cell emitters, older processes
Sources and drains, wells, threshold-voltage adjustment in nearly all modern ICs
when: Thermal diffusion
When the junction is deep, the structure is simple and cost matters, as in some solar cells and power devices.
Ion implantation
When you need precise dose, depth and position, which is the case for transistors in logic and memory.
Together
Implantation puts the dopants in; a high-temperature step then repairs the crystal, activates the dopants and drives them in a little further by diffusion.
faq: Why did ion implantation replace diffusion?
Implantation controls dose and depth precisely, works near room temperature with a simple photoresist mask and can place dopants in very shallow layers.
Why is annealing needed after ion implantation?
Implantation damages the crystal lattice. Annealing repairs the damage and moves the dopants into lattice sites where they become electrically active.
What is channeling?
Channeling is when implanted ions travel unexpectedly deep along gaps in the crystal. Tilting the wafer by a few degrees, or implanting through an amorphous layer, reduces it.
Is thermal diffusion still used?
Yes, for deep junctions and simple structures where cost matters, such as some solar cells and power devices, and to drive dopants deeper after implantation.

cz-vs-fz-silicon.title: CZ vs FZ Silicon: Czochralski and Float-Zone Crystal Growth
cz-vs-fz-silicon.description: CZ vs FZ silicon compared in a table: how each crystal is grown, oxygen content, purity, resistivity, wafer size, cost, strength and typical uses.
cz-vs-fz-silicon.lead: Almost all silicon wafers start as a single crystal grown by one of two methods. In the Czochralski (CZ) method, a seed crystal is dipped into molten silicon in a quartz crucible and slowly pulled up. In the float-zone (FZ) method, a polysilicon rod is melted in a narrow zone by a coil and the zone is moved along the rod, so no crucible touches the silicon. CZ is cheaper and makes large wafers; FZ gives purer silicon.
rows: A seed is dipped into silicon melted in a quartz crucible and pulled up while rotating
A radio-frequency coil melts a narrow zone of a polysilicon rod, and the zone is moved along it
Yes, so oxygen from the quartz dissolves into the melt
No, so there is very little oxygen
Lower purity; resistivity limited (the MCZ variant with a magnetic field helps)
Very high purity and very high resistivity
Dopant is added to the melt; concentration varies along the ingot
Gas doping, or neutron transmutation doping (NTD) for uniform phosphorus
Typically up to about 200 mm; larger sizes are difficult
Lower, and large ingots give good throughput
Oxygen precipitates add strength and trap metal impurities (intrinsic gettering)
Lacks these benefits, so wafers can be more fragile
The large majority of wafers: logic, memory and solar cells
High-voltage power devices (such as IGBTs), detectors, high-resistivity RF devices
when: CZ
The default for mainstream chips. It scales to the largest wafer sizes and is the most economical.
FZ
When high purity and very high resistivity matter more than cost or wafer size, mainly for power devices and sensors.
faq: Why is CZ the most common method?
It is cheaper, produces large ingots (up to 300 mm wafers in production) and gives wafers with oxygen precipitates that add strength and trap impurities.
Why does FZ silicon have higher resistivity?
No crucible touches the silicon, so it picks up very little oxygen and other impurities, which allows very high purity and resistivity.
What is neutron transmutation doping?
Irradiating FZ silicon with neutrons converts some silicon atoms into phosphorus, giving very uniform n-type doping.
What are FZ wafers used for?
High-voltage power devices such as IGBTs, detectors and high-resistivity RF devices.

positive-vs-negative-photoresist.title: Positive vs Negative Photoresist: Differences Explained
positive-vs-negative-photoresist.description: Positive vs negative photoresist compared in a table: reaction to light, pattern polarity, resolution, developer, profile, materials and typical uses.
positive-vs-negative-photoresist.lead: A photoresist is the light-sensitive coating that carries the circuit pattern. With a positive resist, the areas exposed to light become soluble and wash away in the developer, so the pattern matches the mask. With a negative resist, the exposed areas harden and stay, so the pattern is the reverse of the mask. Positive resists dominate fine patterning in chip making, while negative resists are used where thick films or special profiles are needed.
rows: Exposed areas become soluble and are removed by the developer
Exposed areas become insoluble (cross-linked) and remain
Same polarity: the resist pattern copies the mask
Reversed polarity: the resist remains where the mask is clear
Traditionally lower, because the resist can swell in the developer
Usually an aqueous alkaline solution (such as TMAH)
Traditionally an organic solvent; negative-tone development of modern resists also uses solvents
Can be made with an undercut, which helps lift-off processes
Novolac with a diazonaphthoquinone (DNQ) inhibitor; chemically amplified polymers for KrF, ArF and EUV
Cyclized rubber with bis-azide (older); epoxy-based SU-8 for thick MEMS structures
Well suited: SU-8 makes tall, high-aspect-ratio structures
MEMS, lift-off patterning, printed circuit boards, thick layers for packaging, and some special layers in advanced nodes
when: Positive
The default for IC manufacturing, where resolution and well-controlled pattern transfer matter most.
Negative
When you need very thick, tall structures, a lift-off profile, or a specific mask polarity.
faq: What happens to a positive resist when it is exposed?
The exposed area becomes soluble and is dissolved by the developer, so the resist pattern copies the mask.
Why is positive resist preferred for fine patterns?
It offers higher resolution, because negative resists traditionally swell in the developer.
When is a negative resist used?
For thick, tall structures (such as SU-8 in MEMS), for lift-off processes that need an undercut profile, and for some special layers.
What is a chemically amplified resist?
A resist in which exposure creates an acid that triggers many chemical reactions during baking, so a small light dose is enough. It is used for KrF, ArF and EUV lithography.

wire-bonding-vs-flip-chip.title: Wire Bonding vs Flip Chip: Chip Interconnect Compared
wire-bonding-vs-flip-chip.description: Wire bonding vs flip chip compared in a table: how the chip connects, I/O count, electrical performance, cost, size, process and typical uses.
wire-bonding-vs-flip-chip.lead: These are the two main ways to connect a chip to its package. In wire bonding, the chip sits face up and thin metal wires join its edge pads to the package. In flip chip, the chip is turned face down and solder or copper bumps on its surface connect directly to the substrate. Wire bonding is cheap and flexible; flip chip allows many more connections, shorter paths and better electrical performance.
rows: Thin wires (gold, copper or aluminum, roughly 15 to 50 µm) welded from chip pads to the package
Bumps of solder or copper on the chip surface joined directly to the substrate
Pads on the chip edge only; hundreds up to about a thousand connections
Bumps across the whole surface (area array); thousands of connections
Long wires add inductance and resistance, limiting speed and power delivery
Short paths give low inductance and better signal and power integrity
Heat leaves mainly through the back of the chip into the die attach
The back of the chip can touch a heat spreader or heat sink directly
Each wire is bonded one after another, which is slower
All bumps are joined at once by reflow, and underfill resin is added to relieve stress
Larger: space is needed around the chip for the wires
Low: mature, flexible and needs no bumping of the chip
Higher: bumping, a finer substrate and underfill are needed
Memories, microcontrollers, analog chips, LEDs and low-cost products
CPUs, GPUs, SoCs and other high-speed, high-pin-count chips
when: Wire bonding
When the pin count is modest and cost matters most: most microcontrollers, memories and analog parts.
Flip chip
When you need thousands of connections, high speed or high power: processors and high-performance chips.
Note
Flip-chip bumps are also the starting point of advanced packaging, where much smaller micro-bumps join stacked chips.
faq: Why does flip chip allow more connections?
Bumps can be placed across the whole chip surface (an area array), while wire bonding uses only pads at the chip edge, so flip chip can offer thousands of connections.
Is wire bonding obsolete?
No. It is cheap, flexible and mature, and it is still used for most microcontrollers, memories and analog chips.
What is underfill?
A resin filled between a flip chip and its substrate to relieve the stress on the bump joints caused by different thermal expansion.
Which has better electrical performance?
Flip chip, because its connections are short and have low inductance. Long bond wires limit speed and power delivery.

2-5d-vs-3d-packaging.title: 2.5D vs 3D Packaging: Chip Integration Compared
2-5d-vs-3d-packaging.description: 2.5D vs 3D advanced packaging compared in a table: structure, interconnect, bandwidth, heat, complexity, examples such as HBM and CoWoS, and when each is used.
2-5d-vs-3d-packaging.lead: Both approaches put several chips into one package to get more bandwidth than a circuit board can offer. In 2.5D packaging, chips sit side by side on a silicon interposer that wires them together at fine pitch. In 3D packaging, chips are stacked on top of each other and connected through the silicon with through-silicon vias (TSVs) or by hybrid bonding. 3D gives the shortest connections but is harder to cool and to build.
rows: Chips placed side by side on a silicon interposer (or a silicon bridge)
Chips stacked vertically on top of one another
Micro-bumps to the interposer, with very fine wiring layers inside it
TSVs through the chips, joined by micro-bumps or by hybrid bonding
Easier: each chip can be cooled from the top
Harder: heat from lower chips must pass through the chips above
Larger: the interposer must hold all chips
Needs a large interposer, which adds cost
Needs wafer thinning to tens of micrometers, TSV formation and careful testing of each die
AI GPUs with HBM on the same package (such as TSMC CoWoS)
HBM itself (stacked DRAM dies), and stacked cache on a processor
Stacking memory, or stacking logic and cache for the shortest paths
when: When you want to combine a large processor with several memory stacks or chiplets and still cool them easily.
3D
When connection length, power and footprint matter most, as in stacked memory.
Together
High-end AI accelerators use both: HBM is a 3D stack of DRAM dies, placed beside the processor on a 2.5D interposer.
faq: What is a silicon interposer?
A silicon layer with very fine wiring, and often TSVs, that connects several chips placed side by side in 2.5D packaging.
Why is 3D packaging harder to cool?
Heat from the lower chips must pass through the chips stacked above them, while in 2.5D each chip can be cooled from the top.
Is HBM 2.5D or 3D?
Both. HBM is a 3D stack of DRAM dies, and it is placed beside the processor on a 2.5D interposer.
What is a TSV?
A through-silicon via is a vertical connection that passes through a thinned silicon chip, used to link stacked chips.

sem-vs-tem.title: SEM vs TEM: Electron Microscopes in Semiconductor Analysis
sem-vs-tem.description: SEM vs TEM compared in a table: principle, what each shows, resolution, sample preparation, voltage, speed, cost and typical uses in chip analysis.
sem-vs-tem.lead: Both microscopes use a beam of electrons instead of light, but they look at samples in different ways. A scanning electron microscope (SEM) scans a focused beam over the surface and builds an image from the electrons that come back, so it shows the shape of the surface. A transmission electron microscope (TEM) sends electrons through an extremely thin slice, so it can show the inside of the structure down to individual atoms. SEM is fast and easy; TEM is far more powerful but slow and demanding.
rows: A focused beam scans the surface; secondary or backscattered electrons form the image
Electrons pass through a very thin sample; transmitted and diffracted electrons form the image
Internal structure, crystal lattice and atomic-scale interfaces
About 1 nm at best; typically a few nanometers or more
Below 0.1 nm: individual atoms can be seen
Little: bulk samples can be used (insulators need a conductive coating)
Very demanding: the sample must be thinner than about 100 nm, often cut by focused ion beam (FIB)
Line-width measurement (CD-SEM), defect review, cross-section views of devices
Gate-oxide thickness, thin-film stacks, crystal defects and interface structure
when: SEM
For routine inspection and measurement, where speed matters, such as checking patterns and finding defects.
TEM
When you need to see inside a structure at the atomic scale, such as the thickness of a gate dielectric a few atoms thick.
Together
In failure analysis, SEM and FIB find and expose the problem spot, and a thin slice is then cut out for TEM.
faq: Which has higher resolution, SEM or TEM?
TEM. It resolves below 0.1 nm, so individual atoms can be seen, while an SEM resolves about 1 nm at best.
Why does TEM need such a thin sample?
Electrons must pass through the sample, so it must be thinner than about 100 nm. Preparing it, often with a focused ion beam, takes hours.
What does a CD-SEM measure?
A critical-dimension SEM measures the line widths and hole sizes of patterns on wafers. It is a key tool for process control in lithography and etching.
Why are insulating samples coated before SEM?
Insulators build up charge under the electron beam, which distorts the image. A thin conductive coating, or imaging at low voltage, prevents this.

soi-vs-bulk-silicon.title: SOI vs Bulk Silicon: Differences for Chip Makers
soi-vs-bulk-silicon.description: SOI vs bulk silicon wafers compared in a table: structure, isolation, parasitic capacitance, latch-up, back biasing, self-heating, cost and uses.
soi-vs-bulk-silicon.lead: Most chips are built directly in a plain silicon wafer, called bulk silicon. A silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafer adds a thin layer of oxide buried under the thin silicon layer where the transistors sit. That insulating layer isolates the transistors from the substrate, which reduces parasitic capacitance and removes latch-up, so circuits can be faster or lower in power. The price is a more expensive wafer and poorer heat removal.
rows: Transistors are made directly in the silicon wafer
A thin silicon layer sits on a buried oxide (BOX) on a silicon substrate
Complete isolation from the substrate by the BOX, plus trench isolation sideways
Smaller, because the junctions sit on oxide
Possible, because of parasitic thyristor structures
More sensitive to charge from radiation
Less sensitive, because the charge-collection volume is small
Fully depleted SOI (FD-SOI) allows strong back-gate biasing through the BOX
Worse: the oxide layer conducts heat poorly
Most CMOS chips: memory, processors and general logic
RF switches in smartphones, low-power FD-SOI chips for IoT and automotive, MEMS, high-voltage and radiation-tolerant ICs
when: Bulk
The default for mainstream chips, because the wafers are cheap and the ecosystem is mature.
SOI
When low power, RF performance, radiation tolerance or body biasing is worth the extra wafer cost.
faq: What does the buried oxide do?
It insulates the thin silicon layer where the transistors sit from the substrate, which reduces parasitic capacitance and eliminates latch-up.
Why is SOI more expensive?
SOI wafers need extra manufacturing steps to create the buried oxide layer, so they cost substantially more than bulk wafers.
What is FD-SOI?
Fully depleted SOI uses a very thin silicon layer that is completely depleted of carriers. It gives good control of the channel and allows back-gate biasing through the buried oxide.
Why is self-heating worse in SOI?
The buried oxide conducts heat poorly, so heat from the transistors cannot escape into the substrate as easily as in bulk silicon.

igbt-vs-power-mosfet.title: IGBT vs Power MOSFET: Which to Use for What
igbt-vs-power-mosfet.description: IGBT vs power MOSFET compared in a table: structure, voltage range, conduction loss, switching speed, tail current, body diode and typical uses.
igbt-vs-power-mosfet.lead: Both are voltage-controlled power switches with an insulated gate, but they conduct differently. A power MOSFET carries current with one type of carrier and behaves like a resistor, so it is fast and efficient at low and medium voltage. An IGBT adds a bipolar output stage that floods the device with carriers, which keeps conduction loss low at high voltage and current, but makes turn-off slower. The usual split is MOSFETs below a few hundred volts or at high frequency, and IGBTs at high voltage and power.
rows: Unipolar: majority carriers only, controlled by a MOS gate
MOS gate driving a bipolar output stage, so both electrons and holes take part
From a few volts up to about 900 V (silicon); SiC MOSFETs reach several kV
About 600 V up to several kV
Resistive (RDS(on)); rises steeply as the voltage rating increases
Nearly fixed saturation voltage (about 1.5 to 3 V); lower loss at high voltage and high current
Fast: tens or hundreds of kHz, and higher
Slower: usually up to a few tens of kHz
Yes: stored minority carriers keep current flowing briefly
None: a separate antiparallel diode is added in the package
Easy: on-resistance rises with temperature, so current spreads out
Voltage-driven, with gate charge to supply at each switching event
Switching power supplies, DC-DC converters, chargers, low-voltage motor drives
Electric-vehicle inverters (silicon IGBTs), industrial motor drives, trains, welding, grid equipment
when: Power MOSFET
When switching frequency is high and the voltage is not too high: power supplies, converters, battery-powered motor drives.
IGBT
When voltage and current are high and frequency is moderate: traction inverters, industrial drives, heavy equipment.
Trend
SiC MOSFETs are taking over part of the IGBT range, offering high voltage with fast switching and low loss.
faq: When should I choose an IGBT over a MOSFET?
At high voltage and high current (roughly 600 V and above) with a moderate switching frequency, where the low and nearly fixed conduction voltage of an IGBT gives lower loss.
Why is an IGBT slower at turn-off?
Stored minority carriers keep current flowing for a short time after the gate turns off. This tail current limits the switching frequency.
Does an IGBT have a body diode?
No. A separate antiparallel diode is added in the package to carry reverse current.
Are SiC MOSFETs replacing IGBTs?
Partly. SiC MOSFETs offer high voltage with fast switching and low loss, so they are taking over part of the IGBT range, such as electric-vehicle inverters.

sar-vs-delta-sigma-vs-pipeline-vs-flash-.title: SAR vs Delta-Sigma vs Pipeline vs Flash ADC: Architectures Compared
sar-vs-delta-sigma-vs-pipeline-vs-flash-.description: Flash, SAR, pipeline and delta-sigma ADCs compared in a table: how they work, resolution, speed, latency, power, area and typical uses.
sar-vs-delta-sigma-vs-pipeline-vs-flash-.lead: An analog-to-digital converter (ADC) can be built in several ways, and each architecture trades speed against resolution. Flash ADCs are the fastest but only a few bits. SAR ADCs are small, low-power and the general-purpose choice for medium speed. Pipeline ADCs reach high speed with medium-to-high resolution. Delta-sigma ADCs trade speed for the highest resolution, which is ideal for audio and precision sensors.
rows: Compares the input with all thresholds at once using 2ᴺ − 1 comparators
Binary search: one comparator and an internal DAC decide one bit per clock cycle
A cascade of stages, each resolving a few bits and passing an amplified residue to the next
Oversamples with a coarse modulator that shapes noise, then a digital filter produces the output
kS/s up to tens or hundreds of MS/s
10 MS/s up to hundreds of MS/s
Long, because of the digital filter
Grows rapidly with resolution; large and power-hungry
Moderate; the digital filter takes area
High-speed oscilloscopes, optical and wireless receivers, sub-ADC inside pipelines
Microcontroller ADCs, IoT sensors, general data acquisition
Audio codecs, weigh scales, precision measurement
when: Flash
When you need extreme speed and only a few bits, or a fast building block inside another architecture.
SAR
The default for medium speed and medium-to-high resolution, especially when power and size matter.
Pipeline
When you need both high speed and good resolution, as in video and radio receivers.
Delta-sigma
When resolution matters more than speed: audio, scales and low-frequency sensors.
faq: Which ADC architecture is the fastest?
The flash ADC. It compares the input with all thresholds at once and can reach several gigasamples per second, but only with a few bits of resolution.
Why is a delta-sigma ADC so accurate?
It oversamples with a coarse modulator and pushes quantization noise to high frequencies, where a digital filter removes it. This gives 16 to 24 bits of resolution at low speed.
What is a SAR ADC?
A successive-approximation ADC finds the input value by binary search, using one comparator and an internal DAC and deciding one bit per clock. It is small, low-power and common in microcontrollers.
Why does a flash ADC need so many comparators?
An N-bit flash ADC needs 2ᴺ − 1 comparators, for example 255 for 8 bits, so its size and power grow rapidly with resolution.

latch-vs-flip-flop.title: Latch vs Flip-Flop: Differences Explained
latch-vs-flip-flop.description: Latch vs flip-flop compared in a table: triggering, output behavior, construction, size, timing analysis, glitches and when each is used in digital design.
latch-vs-flip-flop.lead: Both store one bit, but they are triggered differently. A latch is level-sensitive: while its enable signal is active it is transparent and passes the input straight to the output, and when the enable goes inactive it holds the value. A flip-flop is edge-triggered: it captures the input only at the clock edge and ignores changes in between. A flip-flop is built from two latches working in opposite phases.
rows: Level-sensitive: acts while the enable is active
Edge-triggered: acts only at the rising or falling clock edge
Follows the input while transparent, then holds
Changes only at the clock edge, stable otherwise
Two latches in series, working in opposite phases (master-slave)
More complex: time borrowing across the transparent phase
Simple: setup and hold times around the clock edge
Glitches and races pass through while transparent
Immune to input changes between clock edges
Custom high-speed designs with time borrowing, clock-gating cells
Registers, counters and state machines in synchronous design
when: Latch
When area, power or speed justify the harder timing analysis, typically in custom or high-performance circuits.
Flip-flop
The default building block in synchronous design, because timing is simple and robust.
HDL tip
In Verilog or VHDL, an incomplete if or case statement in combinational logic creates an unintended latch. Assign a value in every branch to avoid it.
faq: What is the difference between a latch and a flip-flop in one sentence?
A latch is level-sensitive and transparent while its enable is active, while a flip-flop is edge-triggered and captures its input only at the clock edge.
Is a flip-flop made of latches?
Yes. A master-slave flip-flop is two latches in series, working in opposite phases.
Why do designers prefer flip-flops?
Timing analysis is simple, with setup and hold times around one clock edge, and glitches between edges do not matter.
How does an unintended latch appear in HDL code?
When a combinational always block or process does not assign an output in every branch (an incomplete if or case), synthesis keeps the old value and infers a latch.

jfet-vs-mosfet.title: JFET vs MOSFET: Differences Explained
jfet-vs-mosfet.description: JFET vs MOSFET compared in a table: gate structure, normally-on or off behavior, gate current, noise, ESD robustness, integration and typical uses.
jfet-vs-mosfet.lead: Both are field-effect transistors in which a gate voltage controls the current between source and drain. In a MOSFET the gate is insulated by an oxide layer. In a JFET the gate is a reverse-biased PN junction that squeezes the channel. This makes a JFET normally on and gives it very low noise, while the insulated gate of the MOSFET draws almost no current and makes it far easier to integrate by the billions.
rows: A PN junction, which must stay reverse-biased
A metal gate separated from the channel by a thin oxide
Normally on (depletion mode): the gate voltage pinches the channel off
Usually normally off (enhancement mode); depletion types also exist
Small reverse leakage; it rises sharply if the gate is forward-biased
Almost zero in steady state, because of the insulator
Low noise, especially at low frequency
Better, because there is no thin gate oxide to break down
Sensitive: the gate oxide can be destroyed by static discharge
The basis of CMOS: billions of transistors per chip
Low-noise preamplifiers, op-amp input stages, audio and RF front ends, analog switches
Digital logic, memory, power switching and most modern ICs
when: JFET
When low noise and high input impedance matter in an analog front end, such as a microphone or sensor preamplifier.
MOSFET
For nearly everything else: digital circuits, power switching and anything that must be integrated at scale.
faq: Why is a JFET normally on?
Its channel exists with no gate voltage, and a reverse-biased gate junction squeezes it shut. This is depletion-mode behavior.
Which has lower noise, a JFET or a MOSFET?
A JFET, especially at low frequency, which is why it is used in low-noise preamplifier input stages.
Why is a MOSFET more sensitive to static electricity?
Its thin gate oxide can be destroyed by an electrostatic discharge. A JFET has no gate oxide to break down.
Why are MOSFETs used in ICs instead of JFETs?
The insulated gate draws almost no current, and MOSFETs are easy to shrink and to build in complementary pairs (CMOS), so billions fit on one chip.

write-through-vs-write-back-cache.title: Write-Through vs Write-Back Cache: Differences Explained
write-through-vs-write-back-cache.description: Write-through vs write-back cache compared in a table: write policy, memory traffic, speed, consistency, complexity, eviction cost and typical use.
write-through-vs-write-back-cache.lead: A write policy decides what happens when the CPU writes to data that is in the cache. A write-through cache updates the cache and main memory at the same time, so memory is always current but every write costs memory traffic. A write-back cache updates only the cache, marks the line dirty, and writes it to memory later when the line is evicted. Write-back is faster and uses less bandwidth, but it is more complex to keep consistent.
rows: Every write goes to both the cache and the next memory level
A write updates only the cache and sets the dirty bit; memory is updated on eviction
Lower: repeated writes to one line are merged into one write-back
Slower without help; a write buffer hides much of the delay
Faster: writes complete at cache speed
Memory is always up to date, which simplifies sharing with DMA and other cores
Memory can be stale until the line is written back, so coherence needs more care
More complex: dirty bits, write-back on eviction, coherence protocols
Cheap: nothing needs to be written
Evicting a dirty line costs an extra write to memory
Some L1 caches and simple or reliability-focused systems
Most modern CPU caches, especially L2 and L3
when: Write-through
When simplicity and an always-current memory matter more than write bandwidth.
Write-back
When performance matters, especially for code that writes to the same lines many times.
faq: What is a dirty bit?
A bit on each cache line in a write-back cache that marks the line as modified. A dirty line must be written back to memory when it is evicted.
Why is write-back faster?
Repeated writes to the same line stay in the cache and are merged into a single write to memory, which reduces memory traffic.
What does a write buffer do?
In a write-through cache it queues the writes to memory, so the processor does not have to wait for them to finish.
Which is simpler for multiple cores?
Write-through, because memory is always up to date. Write-back needs more care, such as coherence protocols, because memory can be stale.

direct-mapped-vs-set-associative-vs-full.title: Direct-Mapped vs Set-Associative vs Fully Associative Cache
direct-mapped-vs-set-associative-vs-full.description: Direct-mapped, set-associative and fully associative caches compared in a table: where a block can go, tag comparisons, speed, cost, conflict misses and uses.
direct-mapped-vs-set-associative-vs-full.lead: A cache must decide where each block of memory may be stored. In a direct-mapped cache each block has exactly one possible line, which is simple and fast but suffers conflicts when two blocks share a line. In a fully associative cache a block can go anywhere, which avoids conflicts but needs a comparison against every line. A set-associative cache is the compromise: a block can go in any of a few ways within one set. Most CPU caches are set-associative.
rows: Exactly one line, chosen by the index bits
Any of the ways (for example 4 or 8) in one set
All lines at once, in parallel
Highest: a comparator for every line
Reduced as the number of ways grows
None: only compulsory and capacity misses remain
Chosen within the set (LRU or approximations)
Small, simple caches and some microcontrollers
L1, L2 and L3 caches in most CPUs, usually 4 to 16 ways
Small structures such as TLBs and victim caches
when: Direct-mapped
When simplicity, low power and speed matter more than hit rate.
Set-associative
The practical choice for most caches, since a few ways remove most conflict misses at modest cost.
Fully associative
For very small structures where the hit rate is critical and the comparison cost is affordable.
faq: What is a conflict miss?
A miss that happens because two blocks map to the same place even though other cache lines are free. Direct-mapped caches suffer most, and fully associative caches have none.
How many tags does an 8-way cache compare per access?
Eight, one for each way of the selected set.
Why are most CPU caches set-associative?
A few ways remove most conflict misses at a modest cost, while a fully associative cache needs a comparator for every line.
Where is a fully associative cache used?
In small structures such as TLBs and victim caches, where the hit rate matters most and the comparison cost is affordable.

mutex-vs-semaphore.title: Mutex vs Semaphore: Differences Explained
mutex-vs-semaphore.description: Mutex vs semaphore compared in a table: purpose, value, ownership, operations, signaling, priority inversion, typical uses and common pitfalls.
mutex-vs-semaphore.lead: A mutex protects a critical section so that only one thread at a time can use a shared resource, and the thread that locked it must be the one that unlocks it. A semaphore is a counter: it controls how many threads can use a limited resource, and it can also be used to signal events from one thread to another. A mutex is about ownership and exclusion; a semaphore is about counting and signaling.
rows: Mutual exclusion: one thread at a time in a critical section
Counting: limit access to a pool of N resources, or signal events between threads
A non-negative integer count (a binary semaphore is the special case of 0 or 1)
Owned by the thread that locked it, and that thread should unlock it
No owner: any thread can post or signal
Yes: for example a producer signaling a consumer
Protecting a shared data structure such as a list or a counter
Limiting a connection pool, bounded producer-consumer buffers, signaling from an interrupt handler to a task
Deadlock from inconsistent lock order, or forgetting to unlock
Lost signals and deadlock when counts do not match
when: Mutex
When several threads touch the same data and only one may do so at a time.
Semaphore
When you need to limit how many threads use a resource, or to wake a thread when something happens.
faq: Is a mutex the same as a binary semaphore?
Not quite. Both have two states, but a mutex has an owner that must unlock it and often supports priority inheritance, while a semaphore has no owner and can be signaled by any thread.
When do I need a counting semaphore?
When you must limit how many threads use a resource, such as a pool of N connections, or count the available items in a producer-consumer buffer.
What is a deadlock?

A situation where threads wait for each other forever, for example thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Taking locks in a consistent order avoids it.
What is the difference between a spinlock and a mutex?
A spinlock busy-waits and suits very short waits on multicore systems. A mutex puts the waiting thread to sleep, which is better for longer waits.

static-vs-dynamic-linking.title: Static vs Dynamic Linking: Differences Explained
static-vs-dynamic-linking.description: Static vs dynamic linking compared in a table: when linking happens, executable size, memory use, updates, start-up, deployment, performance and typical uses.
static-vs-dynamic-linking.lead: Linking joins your compiled code with the library code it uses. With static linking, the needed library code is copied into the executable at build time, so the program is self-contained. With dynamic linking, the executable only records which shared libraries it needs, and the operating system loads them when the program starts, so many programs can share one copy. Static is simpler to deploy; dynamic saves memory and makes updates easier.
